items.title: Designing a game's UI
items.text: The other pages explain one feature each. This page puts them together into the UI of a whole game: which layer each screen goes on, who opens it, where its data comes from and how the screens share styles and parts. It describes a pattern your game writes itself; the plugin gives you the parts.

items.title: Layer map
items.text:
The default Layer Order has four layers (Documents). Each layer is a CommonUI widget stack: it shows only its top document, and closing that one shows the one below again.

Layer Put there input-mode hide-lower Why UI.Layer.Game The HUD game false The game keeps the keys and the mouse. Nothing is below it to hide. UI.Layer.GameMenu In-game overlays: a map, an inventory menu true, or false to keep the HUD in view The overlay takes the pad and keys while it is open. UI.Layer.Menu The pause menu, settings, other full screens menu true A full screen hides the HUD and the overlays behind it. UI.Layer.Modal Dialogs menu false The screen that asked stays visible behind the dialog.
  • Keep one document per layer where you can. Two HUD documents on UI.Layer.Game do not show together: only the top one shows.
  • A HUD that needs keys of its own, such as one that opens the pause menu, takes one of two input modes:
  • game: game code keeps the key. input-mapping is not allowed with game.
  • all with an input-mapping: the document handles the key. An all document closes on Back, so such a HUD stops back on its <body> (Events).
  • The plugin does not pause the game. Pause it from your own code when the pause menu opens and closes.

items.title: Who opens screens
items.text:
Give the game one owner of its screens: a ULocalPlayerSubsystem of your own, or the PlayerController. It calls UArcRmlViewportSubsystem::OpenDocument and CloseDocument (Documents) and listens to OnDocumentClosed. A sketch:

C++Blueprint MyUISubsystem.h
#pragma once

#include "CoreMinimal.h"
#include "ArcRmlDocumentRef.h"
#include "Host/ArcRmlCloseReason.h"
#include "Subsystems/LocalPlayerSubsystem.h"

#include "MyUISubsystem.generated.h"

UCLASS()
class UMyUISubsystem : public ULocalPlayerSubsystem
{
    GENERATED_BODY()

public:
    virtual void Initialize(FSubsystemCollectionBase& Collection) override;
    void OpenPauseMenu();

private:
    UFUNCTION()
    void HandleDocumentClosed(const FArcRmlDocumentRef& Document, EArcRmlCloseReason Reason);

    void ResumeGame();
};
MyUISubsystem.cpp
#include "MyUISubsystem.h"

#include "Engine/LocalPlayer.h"
#include "Host/ArcRmlViewportSubsystem.h"
#include "MyPauseViewModel.h"

#include UE_INLINE_GENERATED_CPP_BY_NAME(MyUISubsystem)

namespace MyUISubsystem
{
    const FArcRmlDocumentRef PauseMenu{TEXT("/Game/UI/Rml/Screens/PauseMenu/PauseMenu.rml")};
}

void UMyUISubsystem::Initialize(FSubsystemCollectionBase& Collection)
{
    Super::Initialize(Collection);
    UArcRmlViewportSubsystem* Viewport = Collection.InitializeDependency<UArcRmlViewportSubsystem>();
    Viewport->OnDocumentClosed.AddDynamic(this, &ThisClass::HandleDocumentClosed);
}

void UMyUISubsystem::OpenPauseMenu()
{
    UArcRmlViewportSubsystem* Viewport = GetLocalPlayer()->GetSubsystem<UArcRmlViewportSubsystem>();
    TWeakObjectPtr<UArcRmlViewportSubsystem> WeakViewport(Viewport);
    Viewport->OpenDocument(MyUISubsystem::PauseMenu, [WeakViewport](const FArcRmlDocumentRef& Opened)
    {
        UArcRmlViewportSubsystem* Subsystem = WeakViewport.Get();
        UMyPauseViewModel* Model = Subsystem ? Cast<UMyPauseViewModel>(Subsystem->GetViewModel(Opened, TEXT("pause"))) : nullptr;
        if (Model)
        {
            Model->Refresh();
        }
    });
}

void UMyUISubsystem::HandleDocumentClosed(const FArcRmlDocumentRef& Document, EArcRmlCloseReason Reason)
{
    if (Document == MyUISubsystem::PauseMenu && Reason != EArcRmlCloseReason::WorldCleanup)
    {
        ResumeGame();
    }
}

void UMyUISubsystem::ResumeGame()
{
    // Unpause the game here.
}

Besides Core, CoreUObject and Engine, the game module's Build.cs lists ArcRmlUI (the viewport subsystem and the close reason), ArcRmlUIData (FArcRmlDocumentRef) and ModelViewViewModel (the base class of UMyPauseViewModel) in its dependencies.

This is a sketch: it assumes your own UMyPauseViewModel with a Refresh() function.

A PlayerController Blueprint of your game builds the same pattern from these nodes. The sketch assumes your own MyPauseViewModel with a BlueprintCallable Refresh function.

  1. Event BeginPlay, then Arc Rml Viewport Subsystem (in the palette: Get ArcRmlViewportSubsystem) with PlayerController Self, then Bind Event to On Document Closed on it, wired to a custom event HandleDocumentClosed with the inputs Document and Reason.
  2. A custom event OpenPauseMenu: Make Arc Rml Document Ref with Path /Game/UI/Rml/Screens/PauseMenu/PauseMenu.rml, then Open Document for Player with Owning Player Self and that Document.
  3. From its Before Activate pin: Get View Model on the subsystem with the pin's Document and ModelName pause, then Cast To MyPauseViewModel, then its Refresh.

  4. In HandleDocumentClosed: Break Arc Rml Document Ref on Document; when its Path equals the pause menu path and Reason is not WorldCleanup, a Branch resumes the game on True.

  5. FArcRmlDocumentRef has no Blueprint equality node, so the graph compares the Path strings.

  • The Init function, and the BeforeActivate pin of OpenDocumentForPlayer, run on every open that activates the document, after its view models exist and before it shows, so GetViewModel returns them there. AfterActivate fires once the open has succeeded.
  • OnDocumentClosed also fires when a keep-alive document is parked. The reason tells how it closed: Back, DocumentAction (data-action="close"), CloseKey, Api and the others in Documents.

A screen's RML can open the next screen itself with data-action="open:<package path>", a package path. That is enough when the next screen needs nothing from the screen that opens it: its view models come from the sources create, context, resolver or path, and nothing waits for its answer. Pause menu to settings is such a step. Open the screen from game code when:

  • the open starts in gameplay: a key in game input mode, an event, a trigger;
  • the screen needs setup per open, such as the item a vendor shows (Init or SetViewModel);
  • something waits for the answer, as a confirm dialog's caller does;
  • the open has a side effect in the game, such as pausing.

A view model function that a click calls can open a screen too: a parameter named WorldContextObject gets the player controller (Events), from which it reaches your subsystem.

items.title: Choosing a view model source
items.text:
View models has the rules of each source.

I need Use State of this screen only, made fresh on each open (kept while a keep-alive screen is parked) create Data the whole game shares, owned by game code and alive across screens context An instance my C++ makes or finds for the player when the document opens resolver An object game code hands over per open, such as a dialog's message manual with SetViewModel A model my player controller or pawn already holds as a property path To swap the instance while the screen is open settable on any source To run code when the screen closes, such as answering a pending callback on-close

items.title: A typical flow
items.text:
Step Layer Opened by Back HUD UI.Layer.Game Your subsystem, when the player is ready Nothing: game mode takes no Back Pause menu UI.Layer.Menu Your subsystem, from the pause key Closes the pause menu; the HUD shows again Settings UI.Layer.Menu data-action="open:..." in the pause menu Closes settings; the pause menu shows again Confirm dialog UI.Layer.Modal Game code, with a manual model Closes the dialog with reason Back: treat it as cancel
  • The pause menu hides the HUD with hide-lower. Settings opens on the same layer, so the stack shows only settings, and Back returns to the pause menu.
  • The dialog keeps settings visible with hide-lower false, and Back reaches it first because its layer is on top. Its model's on-close can answer the caller when the dialog closes without a choice.
  • The pause menu, settings and an inventory are the screens a player opens again and again. Make them keep-alive, so a reopen keeps scroll and state, and preload them with PreloadDocument so the first open shows at once (Keep-alive and preload). A screen opened once, such as credits, needs neither.

items.title: Tabs or separate documents
items.text:
A frame with tabs (Frames and tabs) fits one screen with sections under a shared header: an inventory, a character sheet and a quest log in one game menu. A visited tab keeps its state until the frame closes, and the frame's head decides the layer, input mode and keep-alive for all of them.

Separate documents fit screens that need their own layer, input mode or keep-alive, and screens opened from several places on their own.

Two things to watch with tabs:

  • A tab is isolated from its frame: frame rules and custom properties do not reach into it, so every tab links the shared style sheets itself.
  • A tab may not declare a view model name that a kept tab declares differently, and a frame cannot have a frame (Frames and tabs). A data-if that rebuilds the arc-embed element drops the kept tabs (Limits).

items.title: Shared parts
items.text:
• Components. A button, a prompt or a list row written once and imported with dc-import by package path (Components). A component file holds markup only. Its styles go in a style sheet of the importing document, so keep them in one shared sheet; an .rcss file with the component's name next to it (Card.rcss) is linked into every document that imports it.
  • One tokens sheet. Colours, spacing and fonts as custom properties on :root, in one sheet linked from every document and every tab (Styling). The fonts themselves come from the Font Sheets setting (Project setup).
  • Key hints. {{ ArcKeys.confirm }}, {{ ArcKeys.back }} and {{ ArcKeys.<Action> }} show the key of the current input device (View models), so one prompt serves keyboard and pad.
  • Input per document. Each screen's own verbs go in its own mapping context, named by input-mapping; Confirm and Back stay in one project-wide context (Input and gamepad).

items.title: Folder layout
items.text:
A game's UI lives under UI/Rml/ of a content root (Project setup). One layout:

Content/UI/Rml/
  Fonts/          Fonts.rcss and the font files
  Shared/         Tokens.rcss and the shared component styles
  Components/     one .rml per component
  Images/         images and icons the documents name
  Screens/
    Hud/          Hud.rml, Hud.rcss
    PauseMenu/    PauseMenu.rml, PauseMenu.rcss
    GameMenu/     the frame and its tabs

The samples keep one folder per screen, with a Shared and a Fonts folder beside them; the demo keeps its screens in one folder with Components and the hub's tabs in subfolders. Screens do not go under UI/Rml/Test/; see Packaging.

items.title: More than one local player
items.text: UArcRmlViewportSubsystem is a local player subsystem, so each local player has its own documents, layers and stack, and your subsystem should be per local player too. For split-screen, see Limits. The ArcRml.* console commands act on the first local player. Details: Screen size, cursor and local players.

items.title: Before you ship
items.text:
• Validate every document on the build machine with -run=ArcRmlValidate -WarningsAsErrors (Validation). It finds missing view model fields, images, fonts and localization keys, and a menu document whose Back action has no key.
  • Walk every screen with the pad only: each one takes focus, every control is reachable by arrow (Navigation), and Back leaves it.
  • Run Sync Strings on your documents, gather and compile the texts, and list the cultures to stage (Localization).
  • Decide which screens are keep-alive: a parked document stays until a discard, a reload or the end of the player's world. Discard a parked screen you will not open again with DiscardDocument (Keep-alive and preload).
  • With Package Everything off, list in Paths to Package the documents your C++ opens by path. The cook adds frames, literal open: targets and documents that Blueprints and data assets reference, and a path that only your C++ names is none of those (Project setup).

items.title: Glossary
items.text: The terms this guide uses, each with the page that explains it. Concepts introduces them in order.

items.title: Component
items.text: An .rml file whose root is <component>, with declared props and slots. A document imports it with <dc-import>, and its markup is expanded into the document when the document is compiled. See Components.

items.title: Content rect
items.text: The part of the screen a document is laid out in. It is the screen without the edges a TV may cut off, no wider than the widest shape the UI may take, and centred; the document's background still fills the whole screen. See Screen size.

items.title: Content root
items.text: The Content folder of the project (/Game) or of a plugin in the project that can contain content (/MyPlugin). Documents and style sheets live in a content root. See Concepts.

items.title: CSS px and dp
items.text: A px in an .rcss file is multiplied by the UE DPI scale (the dp ratio) before layout, so it is one screen pixel only at scale 1.0; dp is multiplied the same way. See Screen size.

items.title: Document
items.text: An .rml file with a <head> and a <body>, styled by .rcss sheets and named by package path, such as /Game/UI/Rml/Menu.rml. It opens per local player. See Documents.

items.title: Field Notify
items.text: Unreal's field notification: a view model property or function marked to broadcast its changes. A document reads only Field Notify fields, and updates when the model broadcasts a change. See Data binding.

items.title: Focus area
items.text: An element with data-focus-area="<name>": an arrow inside it moves only to targets in the same area until focus is told to leave. See Navigation.

items.title: Frame
items.text: A document that shows other documents, its tabs, one at a time in its arc-embed element. It decides the layer and the input mode of its tabs. See Frames and tabs.

items.title: Input mode
items.text: <meta name="input-mode">: game (default) leaves keys and mouse to the game, menu gives them to the document, all gives them to both. See Concepts.

items.title: Keep-alive and park
items.text: A document with <meta name="keep-alive" content="true"> is parked when it closes instead of destroyed: it draws nothing and takes no input, and the next open brings it back as it was left. See Keep-alive and preload.

items.title: Layer
items.text: The UI.Layer.* gameplay tag a document opens on, from <meta name="layer"> (default UI.Layer.Game). Layers stack in the order of the Layer Order setting. See Documents.

items.title: Local player
items.text: One player of the game on this machine; a split-screen game has more than one. A document opens per local player. See Screen size, cursor and local players.

items.title: Package path
items.text: The name of a document or file by its content root and folder, such as /Game/UI/Rml/Menu.rml. See Concepts.

items.title: Preload
items.text: PreloadDocument loads a document, lays it out and parks it before its first open, so that open is fast. See Keep-alive and preload.

items.title: RCSS
items.text: The style sheet language of the plugin, CSS-like, in .rcss files. See CSS support.

items.title: Resolver
items.text: A C++ class derived from UMVVMViewModelContextResolver that creates a view model instance for the resolver source. See Source: resolver.

items.title: RML
items.text: The markup language of documents, HTML-like, in .rml files. See Documents.

items.title: Shipping build
items.text: A packaged build made with Unreal's Shipping configuration. ArcRml.Inspect, the in-game error bar and the sample commands are not in it.

items.title: Source
items.text: Where a view model instance comes from, named by its <viewmodel> declaration: create, context, resolver, manual or path. See Concepts.

items.title: Tab
items.text: A document whose <meta name="frame"> names a frame document; it is shown inside that frame. Opening a tab opens its frame. See Frames and tabs.

items.title: UI action
items.text: An action of the document's Input Mapping Context that fires; the document receives it as a uiaction event with the action's name in ev.action. See UI actions.

items.title: UI update
items.text: One pass of the plugin's UI thread: messages from the game thread, input, bindings, styles, layout and drawing. See The update cycle.

items.title: View
items.text: The loaded instance of a document for one local player: what opens, parks and is discarded. See Keep-alive and preload.

items.title: View model
items.text: An Unreal MVVM view model (UMVVMViewModelBase) a document reads Field Notify fields from and calls functions of. See View models.

items.title: Images
items.text: A document draws an image from a file, from a part of a file, from a sprite sheet, from an SVG, or from a texture asset, and a view model can choose which one. The Images sample shows each way with a caption and swaps two bound images. Run it with ArcRmlSamples.Open Images in the map L_ArcRmlSamples (Samples).

items.title: Image files
Sprite sheets
SVG
Texture assets
items.text:
Images.rml
<img class="im-box" src="asset:/ArcRmlUISamples/UI/Rml/Images/T_Sample_Picture.T_Sample_Picture" width="64" height="64"/>

src="asset:/Package/Path.Object" draws a Texture2D asset, for a picture that should be cooked and compressed like any other texture. The document compile reports an asset: that names a missing asset, another class, or a texture with Virtual Texture Streaming on. A runtime warning is logged for an asset that could not be loaded, loads as another class, has no GPU resource or has no size.

A value that holds {{ }} or var() is not checked by the compile; only the runtime warnings report it.

items.title: Images from a view model
What a packaged build ships
items.text:
• Package Everything on (the default): every png and svg file under a content root ships, except under UI/Rml/Test/ (Packaging).
  • Package Everything off: the images that a shipped document or style sheet names literally ship, and so do the FArcRmlImageRef values that the cook finds in Blueprint class defaults and graph pins, data assets and data tables (Project setup).
  • A literal asset: texture in a shipped document or style sheet is cooked with it. A texture that a view model field references is an ordinary asset reference of the Blueprint or data asset that holds it.

An image path that only runtime data holds is not shipped when Package Everything is off: a plain FString field, in a Blueprint's class defaults or set from C++. Use FArcRmlImageRef or a texture reference, or name the image in a document.

items.title: Drawing is asynchronous
items.text: A file image (<img>, fill-image, an image in a decorator property, a sprite sheet) is decoded in the background and draws nothing until it is ready, typically within one or two drawn frames. An SVG is converted to pixels the same way and keeps the last image while a new size or colour is converted. A file that cannot be decoded logs Could not load texture once.

items.title: Input and gamepad
items.text:
Use this page to make a menu that keyboard and gamepad drive: which keys press, which close, and what the project needs for them.

The GamepadMenu sample is a menu you drive with the keyboard or a gamepad: three buttons, an Info key of the menu's own, and Back, which closes it. The Confirm and Back keys, and the labels the screen shows for them, come from CommonUI, Unreal's UI input framework, so the project needs the input setup; the section below says what it contains.

items.title: The document
The menu's own action
items.text:
input-mapping names a mapping context that the document adds while it is active. IMC_Sample_GamepadMenu maps one action, IA_Sample_MenuInfo, to I and gamepad Y; it arrives as a UI action.

data-hotkey="IA_Sample_MenuInfo" clicks the element when that action fires, so "Info" calls ToggleInfo. {{ ArcKeys.IA_Sample_MenuInfo }} shows the action's key, named by the action's asset name.

Keep Confirm and Back out of a document's mapping context: they belong to one project-wide context.

GamepadMenu/ArcRmlSamplesGamepadMenu.cpp
void UArcRmlSamplesGamepadMenuViewModel::Choose(const FString& Item)
{
    UE_MVVM_SET_PROPERTY_VALUE(LastChoice, FText::FromString(Item));
}

void UArcRmlSamplesGamepadMenuViewModel::ToggleInfo()
{
    UE_MVVM_SET_PROPERTY_VALUE(bInfoShown, !bInfoShown);
}

items.title: A hotkey on the focused row
items.text:
data-hotkey clicks one element on the whole screen. data-hotkey-focus="<action>" clicks only the focused element or the nearest ancestor of it that has the attribute, so one action works on every row of a list. The RowHotkeys sample has three rows; the key marks the row that has focus as the favourite, whichever of its controls is focused:

RowHotkeys.rml
<meta name="input-mapping" content="/ArcRmlUISamples/UI/Rml/RowHotkeys/IMC_Sample_RowHotkeys"/>
RowHotkeys.rml
<div id="rh-row-0" class="rh-row" data-attrif-favourite="Favourite == 0" data-hotkey-focus="IA_Sample_RowAction" data-event-click="call('', 'SetFavourite', 0)">
    <span class="rh-name">Potion</span>
    <button id="rh-use-0" class="rh-use" autofocus="" data-event-click="call('', 'Use', 'Potion'); stopPropagation()">Use</button>
</div>
  • The attribute sits on the row, not on a button inside it. With focus on "Use", the row is the ancestor that has it, and its data-event-click runs as if the row were clicked.
  • The "Use" button ends its click with stopPropagation(), so using it does not also mark the favourite.
  • Only a visible element is clicked. When neither the focused element nor its ancestors have the attribute, data-hotkey and data-hotkey-cycle are tried next.
  • IMC_Sample_RowHotkeys maps IA_Sample_RowAction to R and a press of the right thumbstick; the document's input-mapping meta activates it (the menu's own action).

The code above is an excerpt: the rows "Scroll" and "Gem" are written like "Potion", and the screen also declares its view model.

Run it with ArcRmlSamples.Open RowHotkeys. The readout under the rows starts as Favourite: -1, used:. Press R on the first row: it reads Favourite: 0, used:. Press Down to move to the second row and R again: it reads Favourite: 1, used:. Press Enter on "Use" and used: shows the row's item name.

items.title: Project setup
items.text: The menu needs the CommonUI setup of Project setup, Input for menus, which also lists the sample input assets and their ini lines. A menu document whose Back action has no key logs a warning when it opens, and the validator reports it.

items.title: Run it
items.text:
Play in the map L_ArcRmlSamples, then type in the console:

ArcRmlSamples.Open GamepadMenu

Move with the arrows or the D-pad, press Enter or gamepad A, press I or gamepad Y for "Info", and Esc or gamepad B to close it. ArcRmlSamples.Close closes it too.

items.title: Debugging layout
items.text: The inspector shows what a running document is made of: its element tree, the size and position of one element, and every style rule that reaches it, each with the file and line it came from. Use it when an element has the wrong size, the wrong colour or no effect from a rule you wrote. It exists outside Shipping builds.

items.title: Open it
items.text:
• In a game: open the console and type ArcRml.Inspect <Path> with the package path of an open document, such as /ArcRmlUISamples/UI/Rml/FirstScreen/FirstScreen.rml. The command toggles: the same path closes it, another path moves it to that document, and ArcRml.Inspect without a path closes it. A panel opens at the right of the game viewport and the mouse cursor is shown. While it is open a click in the game viewport picks an element and does not reach the document.
  • In the editor: the Inspect button of the editor preview toolbar picks in the preview, and the Inspector panel shows the result. The preview does not need a game.

Closing the inspector also resets the edits you made in it (see Try a value).

items.title: Pick an element
items.text:
• In the view: move the pointer over the document and the element under it gets a red outline; click to select it. The pick follows geometry only: the topmost element whose border box holds the point. pointer-events: none does not hide an element from it. A ::before or ::after box is not picked: the click selects its parent.

  • In the tree: click a row. The row's element is outlined in the view while the pointer is on the row, and a double click on a row goes to its source line: in the editor it opens the file there, in a game it copies file:line to the clipboard. A row has the tag, then #id and .class names; a text node shows its text in quotes. A dimmed row is not a plain visible element. These are dimmed:

    • text;
    • a generated ::before or ::after;
    • a scrollbar part;
    • an element that is not in the document tree;
    • an element with display: none or visibility: hidden, also through an ancestor.

The selected element is drawn in the view with its content, padding, border and margin boxes.

items.title: Read the selection
items.text:
The panel shows, top to bottom:

  • The element and its source. The label, and the file and line where the element is written. An element that no source line made shows "no source line". In the editor the link opens the file at that line; in a game it copies file:line to the clipboard.
  • The box model. Margin, border and padding widths around the content size, then border box at X, Y, W × H (CSS px, dp ratio R). The values are CSS px as written in a style sheet, not screen pixels: the layout size in screen pixels divided by the dp ratio, the UE DPI scale of the view (Screen size, cursor and players). The border box is where the element sits in the view.
  • The rules. Each rule whose declaration the element uses, by selector with its file and line, and the properties it sets. First comes element style, the inline style, then the rules with the highest specificity first. A rule from user-agent.css is a default every element gets, like a browser's. A group headed inherited from lists the inherited properties the element gets from an ancestor, only the ones the element does not set itself. !important is marked after the value.

Refresh reads the tree and the selection's styles again; press it after the document changed. The tree follows changes of the document by itself.

items.title: Try a value
items.text:
Type a new value into a property field and press ++enter++, or write name: value into the Add a property field and press ++enter++ (a closing ; is accepted). The value goes to the element's inline style in the running document, so you see the result at once. The status line under the buttons answers:

Status Meaning name: value applied The element has the value. The property name is tinted in the list. 'name' is not a known property No property of that name exists. 'value' is not a valid value for 'name' The name exists and the value does not parse. 'name' is ignored by RmlUi The engine accepts the name and drops it. Write the property as name: value The field has no : or no value.

Edits are not written to a file. They stay when the document is rebuilt and are applied to the same element again. Reset edits puts back every original value; closing the inspector does the same. To keep a change:

  1. Press Copy rule on the rule you want to change. It copies that rule's text from the .rcss file with your edits merged in. For the element style, or a rule without a source file, it copies your edits as name: value; lines.
  2. Paste it over the rule in the style sheet. If the file changed since the document loaded, the status line says No rule opens at <file>:<line>; the file changed since it was loaded.

ArcRml.InspectEdit <Path> <selector> <property> <value> does the same without the panel: it selects the first element that matches the selector, applies the edit and logs applied or not applied with the element's tree path. Words after <property> are joined as the value.

items.title: Write a snapshot to the log
items.text:
ArcRml.InspectDump <Path> writes the inspector's view of the selected element to the log, category LogArcRmlUI (in the editor, the Output Log window), after the next UI update of the document. ArcRml.InspectDump <Path> <X> <Y> selects the element at that point of the view (view pixels, not CSS px) first, so it needs no panel. The document has to be open, else the log has ArcRml.InspectDump: '<path>' is not open. The lines, each starting ArcRml.InspectDump::

  • the document title, the element count, the canvas and content rect in pixels and the dp ratio (the UE DPI scale);
  • selected, the element's tree path, its ancestors from the root as tag#id.class, and its source line;
  • the box in view pixels: margin, border, padding, content and the transformed border, the margin, border and padding edges, and the fragment count;
  • every rule as rule '<selector>' at <file>:<line> (specificity N), or rule inline style (specificity N), followed by its properties.

Without a selected element it logs no element selected; a point with no element logs no element of the document at that point. The dump is the form to paste into a bug report, and the only place that prints specificity.

The dump is a console command, so a script that can run console commands can send it, such as a Blueprint Execute Console Command node after the document opened.

items.title: An element has a size of 0 px
items.text:
Select it, in the tree if you cannot find it in the view, and read the content size and the border box.

  • A dimmed row can mean the element is not displayed. Look in the rules for display: none or visibility: hidden, on the element or on an ancestor whose row is dimmed too.
  • A displayed element with 0 in one direction takes that size from its rules, its content or its parent. Look in the rules for width, height, min-* and max-*, and select the parent to read its content size.
  • Type width: 100px or height: 100px into Add a property. If the box grows, the element lacked a size rule.

items.title: Which rule wins
items.text: Each property appears once, under the rule whose value the element uses: a declaration that lost the cascade is not shown. The list puts the element style first, then the rules with the higher specificity; !important is marked after the value. ArcRml.InspectDump prints specificity N for every rule when the order is not enough. A rule you expected is missing from the list when its selector does not match the element, when every property it sets lost to another rule, or when the declaration was dropped as the sheet loaded: the log has a warning for it (Validation).

items.title: A property has no effect
items.text:
1. Is it in the list? A property that is under no rule was dropped at load or never reached the element.
  2. Type it into Add a property. is not a known property and is ignored by RmlUi end the search.
  3. Look the property up in CSS support: parsed, no effect means nothing reads it, and the Not supported list names properties that do not exist.

items.title: An element you cannot pick
items.text:
• It is not displayed or has visibility: hidden: the view's pick skips it. Select it in the tree.
  • Another element is on top of it. Pick the one on top, or select the element in the tree and read its border box.
  • It is a ::before or ::after box: the view selects its parent. Select its row in the tree.

items.title: Keep-alive and preload
items.text: A document is destroyed when it closes, and the next open loads it again from nothing. Two things change that: a keep-alive document is parked when it closes and comes back as you left it, and a preloaded document is loaded before its first open, so that open shows it at once. The KeepAlive sample has a menu with a button for each, and two screens it opens. Run it with ArcRmlSamples.Open KeepAlive in the map L_ArcRmlSamples (Samples).

items.title: Park and reopen
items.text:
Kept.rml
<meta name="keep-alive" content="true"/>

With that <meta> in its <head> (Documents), closing the screen parks it instead of destroying it. Opening it again brings back what the player left:

  • The view model with its values: the count Kept shows is still there. The view model is new only after a discard or a reload.
  • The text in a field, the scroll position of a list, the classes and the data-if state.
  • Loaded images and sounds.

What starts again is focus and the enter animation: focus goes to the autofocus element as on a first open, and the --sound-focus of the element that takes focus plays (Sounds). on-close runs on every park (View models).

A parked document is not open. It draws nothing, takes no input and does not hide the documents below it.

  • A tab cannot declare keep-alive; the <meta> of its frame decides (Frames and tabs).
  • In the editor, a reopen loads the document again when its files changed.
  • In the editor, a reload of documents, style sheets or fonts destroys every parked document.

items.title: Preload
Discard
What you should see
items.text:
Run the sample (Samples). The menu is titled "Keep alive" and has four buttons.

  1. Open kept opens the screen "Kept": a button Add one, the text "Count: 0", a text field and a list "Row 1" to "Row 10".
  2. Add one changes the text to "Count: 1". Type something in the field and scroll the list.
  3. Back parks the screen and shows the menu again. Open kept again shows "Count: 1", your text and the scroll position.
  4. Preload shows nothing new on screen; the log has the preloaded line (What the log says). Open preloaded then shows the screen "Preloaded" at once; its button reads Back closes it.
  5. Discard both also shows nothing new. Open kept now starts at "Count: 0" with an empty field.

items.title: In a Game Feature
items.text: The companion plugin ArcRmlUIGameFeatures, which does not ship with this plugin, has the Game Feature action Preload RML Documents (UArcRmlGameFeatureAction_PreloadDocuments). Its Documents list is preloaded for every local player while the Game Feature is active, and discarded when it deactivates.

items.title: What the log says
items.text:
The lines are in the log category LogArcRmlUI, start with ArcRmlUI: and have Log verbosity, except the failure, a warning. These are the ones to search for:

Line Meaning preload '<path>' queued, <n> pending PreloadDocument queued the path. preloaded '<path>' view <id> ...; it is parked for its first open The document is loaded and parked. preload of '<path>' view <id> failed; the view is destroyed (warning) The preload failed; the next open loads the document cold. open '<path>' requested before its preload was sent; it opens cold An open came first and dropped the queued preload. discarded the parked|preloading '<path>' view <id>: <reason> A parked or still preloading view was destroyed. The reason names the cause, for example discard requested, documents, style sheets or fonts reloaded, its compiled file is stale or its world is cleaned up. discard '<path>' ignored, it is not parked Nothing was destroyed: the path is not parked and not a kept screen that is closing.

items.title: Limits
items.text: What a document and a view model cannot do. Most limits come with a way around them. This page says what is possible or not here; for things going wrong, see Troubleshooting.

items.title: Binding
items.text:
• An expression reads one model: the nearest data-model ancestor. To combine two, nest an element with the second data-model.
  • call() cannot pass an object of another model. An argument 'vm:<path>' resolves in the model of the calling element.
  • Expressions cannot build arrays or loop counts. Use a fixed cell per index.
  • data-if and data-for on one element: an error is logged and data-for is kept. Nest two elements. The validator reports it as structural-conflict (Validation).
  • data-if rebuilds its branch on every change from false to true, so focus, scroll and hover state inside it are lost.
  • data-action needs a data-model on the <body> of the document or the tab; without it a click warns and does nothing.
  • Model variables are read-only: data-value cannot write an input back to a view model. Call a function that sets the field (View models).
  • A virtual list (data-virtual) needs a parent that scrolls vertically and rows of one size; a row that leaves the window loses focus, hover and animations, and its two spacer elements count in :nth-child (Data binding).
  • data-rml escapes nothing: markup in the string becomes elements, so never put text a player typed in it (Data binding).
  • An alias is resolved once, when its element is created, and a model variable of the same name hides it (Data binding).

items.title: Input and focus
items.text:
• Tab moves nothing in a document with focus areas, except in a focused text field. Arrows move focus (Navigation).
  • A non-form element needs tab-index: auto; nav: auto to take focus by arrow; without nav an arrow does nothing and sends no navnotarget, the event for an arrow that finds no target (Navigation).
  • Duplicate hotkeys and cycles: the one on the focus chain wins, else the first visible one in the focused area, then in the document, with no diagnostic (Navigation).
  • A text field types from the moment it takes focus; pad back ends typing, and Left and Right at the ends of the caret move focus (Text fields).
  • A drag is cancelled when its source or an ancestor is removed (a data-if turning false), the pointer capture is lost or a new press arrives (Drag and drop).

items.title: Style
items.text:
• A leave animation is cut off after LeaveTimeoutSeconds (default 0.5 s; Leave Timeout Seconds in Project Settings > Game > ArcRmlUI, see Settings), and @starting-style rules are dropped (Styling).
  • data-pulse-* does not pulse on the first value or in a view created by the change; use keyed rows in a data-for (Styling).
  • Only the whole text of an element is localized: no child element or {{ }} in a loc element, and no text in an attribute (Localization).
  • Part of CSS is not supported: position: sticky, columns, clip-path and others are dropped with a warning. Find the way around in CSS support and Tailwind CSS.
  • data-world places the element from the screen origin: its own layout position must be the top-left corner, and a transform of your own goes on a child (World markers).

items.title: Lifecycle
items.text:
• A tab is isolated from its frame: frame rules and custom properties do not reach into it, and its :root and html rules refer to the tab. A data-if that rebuilds the frame's arc-embed drops the kept tabs (Frames and tabs).
  • A parked document stays until a discard: there is no eviction, and DiscardDocument is C++ only (Keep-alive and preload).

items.title: Platform
items.text:
• No accessibility support: a document exposes nothing to a screen reader or the Slate accessibility system, and there is no text size setting of its own. The size option is the UI scale, which scales px for every document (Screen size, cursor and players).
  • Split-screen is not supported yet, and has not been run. Each local player has its own layers and documents, but the DPI scale that sizes px comes from the whole viewport, not from that player's part of the screen (Screen size, cursor and players).
  • The runtime is Win64 only for now. Other platforms are not supported yet.

items.title: Localization
items.text:
Use loc to put the texts of a screen into a String Table. The game can then change language without a second set of documents.

The Localization sample has a panel whose texts come from a String Table and change language in place. Two buttons ("English", "Polski") switch the culture. The title, the sentences, the labels and the "Add a coin" button change at once, and the plain line never does. "Add a coin" counts up, and the count picks its plural form for the current language: "1 coin", "2 coins" in English, "1 moneta", "2 monety", "5 monet" in Polish. Run it with ArcRmlSamples.Open Localization in the map L_ArcRmlSamples (Samples).

items.title: loc
items.text:
loc="Key" on an element that holds plain text makes the text the entry Key of the document's String Table. The text written in the .rml is the source (English) text. A key is made of A-Z, a-z, 0-9, _, . and -.

Localization.rml
<h1 class="lc-title" loc="Title">Localization</h1>
<p class="lc-text" loc="Welcome">Welcome, traveler!</p>
<p class="lc-plain">Plain text without loc stays as written.</p>
<button id="lc-add" class="lc-button" loc="AddCoin" data-event-click="call('', 'AddCoin')">Add a coin</button>
  • The table is one per .rml file: <folder>/Loc/ST_<Name> beside the file, here Loc/ST_Localization. Only UStringTable assets named ST_* in a Loc folder under a content root are loaded.
  • A text without loc is shown as written in every culture.
  • On a component, put loc-<prop> on its dc-import instead of loc, which is an error there (Components). <dc-import name="/Game/UI/Rml/Components/Card" loc-title="CardTitle"/> takes the text of the prop title from the entry CardTitle in the table of the importing file. A loc inside the component uses the component's own table.
  • A key with no entry shows the key and warns once; the validator reports it as missing-loc-key.

items.title: Plurals
items.text:
{{ n | arcplural('Key') }} takes the entry Key of the same table, which holds the forms. The entry is String Table text, not RML:

Localization.rml
<span id="lc-coins" class="lc-value">{{ Coins | arcplural('Coins') }}</span>
String Table entry Coins
{0}|plural(one={0} coin,other={0} coins)

The forms are zero, one, two, few, many and other; other is required, and the form the current language picks must exist. {0} is the number. The Polish entry adds few and many. You edit the entry in the String Table itself; Sync Strings only checks it.

items.title: The culture switch
Edit the texts
items.text:
1. Change the text in Localization.rml, then right-click the file (or its folder) in the Content Browser and choose Sync Strings. It adds new keys to ST_Localization and updates changed texts; a folder syncs every .rml under it. Nothing is ever removed from a table. From editor Python the same function is unreal.ArcRmlStringSyncLibrary.sync_strings([...]), which takes the package path of each document and returns the errors as <path>(<line>): <message>.
  2. Gather, translate and compile with the project's Game localization target. The String Table is a content asset, so the target can gather it. Open Tools > Localization Dashboard, select the Game target and, in its settings, enable Gather from Packages and add an include path that covers your documents (the default Game target gathers no packages). Click Gather Text, translate the texts (the edit-translations button in the culture's row, or the exported .po file), then click Compile Text.

The dashboard lists only the Game and Engine targets, not a plugin's LocalizationTargets. For the samples' plugin target, run this from the project folder instead (where UnrealEditor-Cmd.exe is):

UnrealEditor-Cmd.exe "<Project>.uproject" -run=GatherText -config=Plugins/ArcRmlUISamples/Config/Localization/ArcRmlUISamples.ini

It exports Content/Localization/ArcRmlUISamples/<culture>/ArcRmlUISamples.po. Write the translations as the msgstr lines of pl/ArcRmlUISamples.po and run the same command again: it imports the .po and compiles Content/Localization/ArcRmlUISamples/<culture>/ArcRmlUISamples.locres.

items.title: Packaging
items.text:
A packaged game ships only the cultures listed in the project's packaging settings. In Config/DefaultGame.ini:

[/Script/UnrealEd.ProjectPackagingSettings]
+CulturesToStage=pl

Limits

  • Only the whole text of an element is localized: a loc element holds no child element and no {{ }}, or the compile fails. A text in an attribute (a tooltip, a placeholder) cannot be localized; it stays as written.
  • Sync Strings never writes an arcplural entry; a missing or bad one is an error in its report.

items.title: Navigation reference
items.text: The rules behind Navigation: focus areas, leaving an area, redirecting an arrow, containing focus, navnotarget, Back and the parent area, the tab bar and focus requests. The tutorial builds one screen from the BackAndParent sample; the samples quoted here are FocusAreas, BackAndParent, TabBar and FocusRequest (Samples).

items.title: Focus areas
items.text:
data-focus-area="<name>" makes an element one area: an arrow inside it picks only targets in the same area. data-focus-primary marks the area that gets focus first, and autofocus on one of its elements is where it lands. A document whose focus is nowhere moves nothing on the first arrow, so give the entry element autofocus.

FocusAreas.rml
<div class="fa-area" data-focus-area="left">
    <p class="fa-label">left</p>
    <button id="fa-left-1" class="fa-item">Left 1</button>
    <button id="fa-left-2" class="fa-item">Left 2</button>
</div>
<div class="fa-area" data-focus-area="middle" data-focus-primary="">
    <p class="fa-label">middle (primary)</p>
    <button id="fa-middle-1" class="fa-item" autofocus="">Middle 1</button>
    <button id="fa-middle-2" class="fa-item">Middle 2</button>
</div>

A <button> is a navigation stop by default. A div or span needs tab-index: auto; nav: auto.

items.title: Leaving an area
items.text:
At the edge of an area an arrow moves focus to the nearest item of another area. This needs nav-<direction>: auto on the focused element for that direction; buttons and other form controls get it from the default style sheet. #id moves focus to the named element wherever it is, in this area or another. Any other value (none, tree-order, horizontal, vertical) or no nav at all never leaves the area. Focus does not wrap around.

Limits

  • A non-form element without tab-index: auto; nav: auto takes no arrow: nothing moves and no navnotarget is sent.
  • Tab moves nothing in a document with focus areas, except in a focused text field.

items.title: Redirecting an arrow
items.text:
Two attributes on an area take an arrow before the spatial search.

data-nav-left, -right, -up and -down hold a selector. When focus is inside the area and that arrow is pressed, the first visible element in the area that matches is clicked and focus does not move. A selector with no visible match logs a warning and the arrow still moves nothing. A quantity row that steps with Left and Right: <div data-focus-area="details" data-nav-left="#qty-minus" data-nav-right="#qty-plus">, where #qty-minus and #qty-plus are the row's step buttons.

data-focus-down="<area>" makes Down enter that area; an empty value enters the primary area. Only Down is redirected: <div data-focus-area="bar" data-focus-down="list"> sends Down from the bar into the area list.

items.title: Containing focus
items.text:
data-focus-contain makes an area and every area inside it one container. A leave from inside targets only the other areas of the container, never outside it. Use it for a popup.

FocusAreas.rml
<div class="fa-popup" data-focus-area="popup" data-focus-contain="">
    <p class="fa-label">popup (data-focus-contain)</p>
    <div class="fa-columns">
        <div class="fa-area" data-focus-area="popup-a">
            <p class="fa-label">popup-a</p>
            <button id="fa-popup-a" class="fa-item">Popup A</button>
        </div>
        <div class="fa-area" data-focus-area="popup-b">
            <p class="fa-label">popup-b</p>
            <button id="fa-popup-b" class="fa-item">Popup B</button>
        </div>
    </div>
</div>

Left and Right move between popup-a and popup-b; no arrow leaves the popup.

items.title: When an arrow finds nothing: navnotarget
items.text:
When the search for an arrow finds no target in the area, the document sends navnotarget to the focused element. It bubbles and can be cancelled. Its parameters:

Parameter Value ev.direction left, right, up or down ev.area the data-focus-area of the focused element's area, '' outside one ev.target_area the area focus is about to leave into, '' when there is none FocusAreas.rml
<body data-model="areas" data-event-navnotarget="call('', 'NoTarget', ev.direction, ev.area, ev.target_area)">

stopPropagation() cancels the move and focus stays. "Right 2" stops Down only; Down there would leave into the popup, and Left still bubbles to <body>:

FocusAreas.rml
<button id="fa-right-2" class="fa-item" data-event-navnotarget="callIf(ev.direction == 'down', '', 'Cancelled', ev.direction, ev.area, ev.target_area); stopPropagation(ev.direction == 'down')">Right 2 (stops Down)</button>

navnotarget is sent only when the focused element's nav-<direction> for that arrow is auto, tree-order, or horizontal / vertical along the arrow's own axis. It is not sent when a listener or a control already handled the key, such as a caret move in a text field or an open select.

items.title: Back and the parent area
items.text:
Back (see Events) in a child area returns focus to its parent area, even when <body> handles Back. Back in an area without a parent goes on to the elements around the area, up to <body>, and closes the document when no handler stops it. The BackAndParent sample has a list area and a detail area:

BackAndParent.rml
<body data-model="back" data-event-back="call('', 'CountBack')">
    <div class="bp-area" data-focus-area="list" data-focus-primary="">
        <button id="bp-sword" class="bp-item" autofocus="" data-event-click="call('', 'Select', 'Sword')">Sword</button>
    </div>
    <div class="bp-area" data-focus-area="detail" data-focus-parent="list" data-focus-exit="#bp-done">
        <button id="bp-use" class="bp-item" data-event-click="call('', 'Use')">Use</button>
        <button id="bp-done" class="bp-item" data-event-click="call('', 'Exit')">Done</button>
    </div>
</body>

The block is an excerpt: the buttons "Shield" and "Potion" of list are left out.

  • data-focus-parent="list": Back in detail returns focus to the list item that the arrow left from. The item is remembered only when focus entered detail by a leave from list.
  • data-focus-exit="#bp-done": when Back leaves detail, the first match of the selector is clicked, so Exit runs. A direct click on "Done" runs Exit too but does not leave the area.
  • data-event-back on <body> hears every Back that is not a return to a parent area. It does not call stopPropagation(), so a Back in list still closes the document.

The order of one Back:

  1. The document's back sound plays, if a style sheet declares one (Sounds).
  2. If a drag is being carried, it is cancelled and the Back ends (Drag and drop).
  3. Else, if an area entry is pending, it is cancelled and the Back ends.
  4. The back event runs from the focused element up to its area. A handler there that stops it handles the Back.
  5. If the area has a data-focus-parent that exists and has something to focus, focus returns to it.
  6. Otherwise the event goes on to the elements above the area, up to <body>. A handler that stops it handles the Back.
  7. Otherwise the document closes.

Each handler runs at most once per Back. A parent that is missing, has nothing to focus or is the area itself counts as no parent, so a screen needs only one handler on <body> and a data-focus-parent on each child area. With nothing focused, the Back starts at the active area, as if focus were in it.

items.title: Back from game code
items.text:
UArcRmlViewportSubsystem::PostBack(Document) is BlueprintCallable and posts the same Back as the key. The sample's "Back" button, outside every area, calls it from its view model; the WorldContextObject is the player controller (World context object):

BackAndParent/ArcRmlSamplesBackAndParent.cpp
void UArcRmlSamplesBackAndParentViewModel::PressBack(UObject* WorldContextObject)
{
    const APlayerController* Player = Cast<APlayerController>(WorldContextObject);
    const ULocalPlayer* LocalPlayer = Player ? Player->GetLocalPlayer() : nullptr;
    UArcRmlViewportSubsystem* Viewport = LocalPlayer ? LocalPlayer->GetSubsystem<UArcRmlViewportSubsystem>() : nullptr;
    if (Viewport)
    {
        Viewport->PostBack(ArcRmlSamplesBackAndParent::Document);
    }
}

The excerpt is the one function. ArcRmlSamplesBackAndParent::Document is the FArcRmlDocumentRef of BackAndParent.rml, declared in the same file. PostBack returns false and posts nothing when the document is not open, is leaving, its view is hidden, its input-mode is game or its view takes no input.

items.title: Tab bar
items.text:
The TabBar sample has three tabs and a content area for each. data-hotkey-cycle="<previous> <next>" on the bar names two UI actions of the document's input mapping context (IA_Sample_PrevTab, IA_Sample_NextTab: Q and E, gamepad shoulders); Input and gamepad shows how a document names its mapping context.

TabBar.rml
<meta name="input-mapping" content="/ArcRmlUISamples/UI/Rml/TabBar/IMC_Sample_TabBar"/>
TabBar.rml
<div class="tb-bar" data-focus-area="bar" data-focus-primary="" data-hotkey-cycle="IA_Sample_PrevTab IA_Sample_NextTab">
    <button id="tb-tab-items" class="tb-tab" autofocus="" data-attrif-selected="Selected == 0" data-focus-enter="items" data-event-click="call('', 'Select', 0)">Items</button>
    <button id="tb-tab-skills" class="tb-tab" data-attrif-selected="Selected == 1" data-focus-enter="skills" data-event-click="call('', 'Select', 1)">Skills</button>
    <button id="tb-tab-map" class="tb-tab" data-attrif-selected="Selected == 2" data-focus-enter="map" data-event-click="call('', 'Select', 2)">Map</button>
</div>
<div class="tb-content" data-if="Selected == 0" data-focus-area="items">
    <p class="tb-label">Items</p>
    <button id="tb-items-sword" class="tb-item">Sword</button>
    <button id="tb-items-shield" class="tb-item">Shield</button>
</div>

  • The items of the cycle are the visible descendants of the bar with tab-index: auto (here the three buttons). The step wraps from the last to the first.
  • The current item is the one that contains the focus, else the first with the selected attribute, which the view model keeps with data-attrif-selected. A value that is not exactly two names is a validator error.
  • Focus in the bar: the next tab is focused and then clicked, so Select runs like a mouse click. data-focus-enter="items" on the tab sends focus into the area items once Select has run and the area is shown, and it lands on the area's autofocus element, else its first item.
  • Focus outside the bar, in a content area: the key only clicks the tab after the selected one, and that click's data-focus-enter decides where focus goes.
  • data-focus-enter is read only from a click (a mouse click, gamepad accept or a cycle step), never from a key handler that calls the view model.

Limits

  • A cycle item whose data-focus-enter names an area that also exists in the tab shown now enters that old area. An entry for an area that never appears waits until the next arrow, Enter or Space key; the first Back only cancels it.
  • When several elements have the same data-hotkey or data-hotkey-cycle, the first match of this lookup is used:
    1. The focused element, or its nearest ancestor that has it.
    2. The first visible one in document order in the focused area.
    3. The first visible one in document order in the document.

A hotkey on the action wins over a cycle. A second cycle on the same actions (a sub-tab bar, say) steps when focus is inside it; otherwise the first in that order steps. - A custom "disabled" element must drop its tab-index itself; only a disabled form control gets focus: none.

items.title: Focus requests
items.text:
data-focus-request="<field>" on a focusable element moves focus to it when the view model changes the bound value. The FocusRequest sample has three "Go to" buttons, each bumping a counter that one text field binds:

FocusRequest.rml
<button id="fr-go-name" class="fr-button" autofocus="" data-event-click="call('', 'FocusName')">Go to name</button>
<input id="fr-name" class="fr-field" type="text" data-focus-request="NameFocusSerial"/>
  • The first value never focuses. Every later change to a value that is not empty focuses the element, so a view model adds 1 to an int32 for each request.
  • The focus moves like a navigation move: the element gets :focus-visible, scrolls into view, and its focus area becomes the active one. Focus areas do not confine it, so a request can leave the area focus is in.
  • A request on an element that is hidden, disabled or not focusable does nothing. Several requests before one frame give one move to the last element.
  • It is the web's element.focus() for a focus the game starts, for example the first invalid field after a failed submit. A focused text field takes typing again.

Run it with ArcRmlSamples.Open FocusRequest.

items.title: Run it
items.text: Play in the map L_ArcRmlSamples and type ArcRmlSamples.Open FocusAreas, ArcRmlSamples.Open BackAndParent or ArcRmlSamples.Open TabBar in the console; ArcRmlSamples.Close closes the document.

items.title: Navigation
items.text:
Use this page when a screen has more than one button or region and arrows or the D-pad must move between them predictably.

Arrows and the D-pad move focus between the elements of a menu. A document with several regions groups them in focus areas, so the focus stays in a region until it is told to leave. Three samples show it: FocusAreas, BackAndParent and TabBar. The keys and the project's input setup are in Input and gamepad. Run one with ArcRmlSamples.Open <Sample> in the map L_ArcRmlSamples (Samples). The attribute details are on Navigation reference.

items.title: In short
items.text:
• An arrow moves focus to the nearest item in the same data-focus-area; at the area's edge it leaves to another area.
  • data-focus-primary and autofocus decide where focus starts; a non-form element needs tab-index: auto; nav: auto to take an arrow.
  • data-focus-contain keeps focus inside a popup; navnotarget reports an arrow that found no target in its area, before focus leaves it.
  • Back in a child area returns to its parent area (data-focus-parent) before the document closes.
  • data-hotkey-cycle steps a tab bar and data-focus-request moves focus from the view model.

items.title: How focus works
items.text:
One screen of the FocusAreas sample shows how the attributes combine. It has the areas left, middle and right and a popup with the areas popup-a and popup-b:

  1. middle has data-focus-primary, so the document opens there, on its autofocus button (Middle 1).
  2. An arrow moves between the buttons of middle. At its edge, Left moves to the nearest item of left: that is a leave.
  3. Inside the popup, data-focus-contain limits a leave to popup-a and popup-b; no arrow gets out.
  4. When an arrow finds no target in its area, the focused element gets navnotarget before focus leaves the area. A handler that stops it cancels the leave (the button "Right 2" does it for Down).
Attribute or event Role Section data-focus-area, data-focus-primary Group elements; the area that gets focus first Focus areas nav-<dir> Lets an arrow leave an element's area Leaving an area data-nav-<dir>, data-focus-down Take an arrow before the spatial search Redirecting an arrow data-focus-contain One container of areas that focus never leaves Containing focus navnotarget An arrow found no target in its area; stopping it cancels the leave navnotarget data-focus-parent, data-focus-exit Back returns to a parent area Back and the parent area data-focus-enter A tab click sends focus into an area Tab bar data-focus-request The view model moves focus to an element Focus requests data-focus-owner Marks the container of a popup and its trigger; on blur, ev.related_in_owner is true when focus moves to an element inside that container (Event reference) Attributes

Navigation reference gives each rule in full; the tutorial below builds one screen.

items.title: Tutorial: a list and a detail
items.text: The BackAndParent sample is one screen with two areas: list (Sword, Shield, Potion) and detail (Use, Done). The steps below build it. Each step names the rule it uses; the full rule is in Navigation reference.

items.title: 1. Mark the areas
items.text:
data-focus-area="<name>" makes an element one area: an arrow inside it picks only targets in the same area. data-focus-primary on list makes it the area that gets focus first, and autofocus on "Sword" is where it lands (Focus areas).

BackAndParent.rml
<div class="bp-area" data-focus-area="list" data-focus-primary="">
    <button id="bp-sword" class="bp-item" autofocus="" data-event-click="call('', 'Select', 'Sword')">Sword</button>
</div>
<div class="bp-area" data-focus-area="detail" data-focus-parent="list" data-focus-exit="#bp-done">
    <button id="bp-use" class="bp-item" data-event-click="call('', 'Use')">Use</button>
    <button id="bp-done" class="bp-item" data-event-click="call('', 'Exit')">Done</button>
</div>

A <button> is a navigation stop by default. The list also holds the buttons "Shield" and "Potion", written like "Sword". data-focus-parent and data-focus-exit on detail are step 3.

items.title: 2. Move between the areas
items.text: Up and Down move between the buttons of list. Right from a list item is at the edge of list, so focus leaves to the nearest item of detail. A button may leave in any direction because it has nav: auto from the default style sheet (Leaving an area).

items.title: 3. Go back
items.text:
Back (Esc or gamepad B, see Events) is the key or pad button that closes a menu. Two attributes on detail give it a way back:

  • data-focus-parent="list": Back in detail returns focus to the list item that the arrow left from. The item is remembered only when focus entered detail by a leave from list.
  • data-focus-exit="#bp-done": when Back leaves detail, the first match of the selector is clicked, so Exit runs. A direct click on "Done" runs Exit too but does not leave the area.

Back in list, which has no parent, goes on to <body> and closes the document when no handler stops it. The sample's <body data-event-back="call('', 'CountBack')"> hears every Back that is not a return to a parent area. It does not call stopPropagation(), so a Back in list still closes the document. The order of one Back is in Back and the parent area.

items.title: 4. Back from a button
items.text: The sample's "Back" button lies outside every area. Its click calls PressBack in the view model, which posts the same Back as the key with PostBack, so it closes the document (Back from game code).

items.title: 5. Run it
items.text:
Play in the map L_ArcRmlSamples and type ArcRmlSamples.Open BackAndParent in the console. Right moves focus from "Sword" to "Use" in detail; press Back (Esc or gamepad B) to return to the list, press Back again to close the document. The counters on the screen show the backs heard and the clicks on "Done" and "Use". ArcRmlSamples.Close closes the document.

Not in this sample: containing focus and navnotarget (FocusAreas), redirecting an arrow, the tab bar (TabBar) and focus requests (FocusRequest).

items.title: Project setup
items.text: What a project needs before it opens its first ArcRmlUI document. A document that only shows information (input-mode game, as in the Quick start) needs the plugin and a font; a menu that takes keys and the gamepad also needs the input setup.

items.title: Requirements
items.text:
• Unreal Engine 5.8.
  • Win64 is the only supported platform. Other platforms are not supported yet.
  • The plugins ArcRmlUI turns on with itself: UMG Viewmodel (ModelViewViewModel), Common UI Plugin and Enhanced Input; in the editor also Content Browser - File Data Source and GameplayTagsEditor.

items.title: Enable the plugin
items.text:
Add ArcRmlUI to your project from Fab (Add to Project) or install it to the engine, then enable it in Edit > Plugins. It enables the plugins above with itself.

A C++ module that opens documents or defines view models lists the plugin's modules in its Build.cs: ArcRmlUIData holds FArcRmlDocumentRef, ArcRmlUI the viewport subsystem. Opening documents needs only those two. This excerpt of the samples module's Build.cs also lists the modules its view models use:

ArcRmlUISamples.Build.cs
        PublicDependencyModuleNames.AddRange(
            new string[]
            {
                "Core",
                "CoreUObject",
                "Engine",
                "ArcRmlUIData",
                "ModelViewViewModel",
                "FieldNotification"
            }
        );

        PrivateDependencyModuleNames.AddRange(
            new string[]
            {
                "ArcRmlUI",
                "UMG"
            }
        );

items.title: Where documents live
items.text: .rml and .rcss files live in the Content folder of the project or of a plugin in the project's Plugins folder that can contain content, and are named by package path: /Game/UI/Rml/Menu.rml is Content/UI/Rml/Menu.rml of the project. The guide and the samples keep them under UI/Rml/. They show in the Content Browser next to the assets.

items.title: Fonts
items.text:
ArcRmlUI ships no font. A project declares its fonts in font sheets: style sheets with @font-face rules, loaded at start; their fonts serve every document. The samples' font sheet:

Fonts/Fonts.rcss
@font-face {
    font-family: 'Arc Samples Sans';
    src: /ArcRmlUISamples/UI/Rml/Fonts/AtkinsonHyperlegible-Regular.ttf;
}

In Project Settings > Game > ArcRmlUI > Fonts (Config/DefaultGame.ini, section [/Script/ArcRmlUI.ArcRmlUISettings]):

Setting ini key What it does Font Sheets +FontSheets=/Game/UI/Rml/Fonts/Fonts.rcss One line per font sheet, by package path. Fallback Font Family FallbackFontFamily= The family text is drawn with when no style sets one. Generic Font Families GenericFontFamilies= Maps a generic name such as sans-serif to a declared family.

These settings take effect after an editor restart.

items.title: Layers
items.text: A document opens on a layer, a UI.Layer.* gameplay tag named by <meta name="layer">; Documents explains them. The plugin defines four tags, UI.Layer.Game, UI.Layer.GameMenu, UI.Layer.Menu and UI.Layer.Modal, listed bottom to top in that order by default. A document that names a layer missing from the order is an error; the order is Project Settings > Game > ArcRmlUI > Layers > Layer Order.

items.title: Input for menus
items.text:
A document with input-mode menu or all takes keys through CommonUI:

  • Confirm is always Enter, Space or the gamepad's accept button, and presses the focused element. The click action of the CommonUI input data only supplies the key label a document shows for Confirm.
  • Back is the back action of the CommonUI input data. A Back that no handler stops closes the document.

So the project needs its own Confirm and Back actions, one project-wide mapping context and the CommonUI input data that names the two actions:

  1. Make the game use the CommonUI viewport client: in Project Settings > Engine > General Settings > Default Classes set Game Viewport Client Class to CommonGameViewportClient (GameViewportClientClassName in [/Script/Engine.Engine]).
  2. In Project Settings > Engine > Input > Default Classes set Default Player Input Class to EnhancedPlayerInput and Default Input Component Class to EnhancedInputComponent.
  3. In the Content Browser create two Input Actions (Input > Input Action), for example IA_Confirm and IA_Back.
  4. Create an Input Mapping Context (Input > Input Mapping Context). Map Enter, Space and the gamepad's bottom face button to Confirm, Esc and the gamepad's right face button to Back. These keys are also the labels a document shows for Confirm and Back.
  5. Add the context in Project Settings > Engine > Enhanced Input > Default Mapping Contexts with Add Immediately on.
  6. In Project Settings > Game > Common Input Settings turn on Enable Enhanced Input Support and restart the editor; the Blueprint's Enhanced Input fields stay hidden until then.
  7. Create a Blueprint class with the parent Common UI Input Data. Set its Enhanced Input Click Action to IA_Confirm and its Enhanced Input Back Action to IA_Back.
  8. In Common Input Settings set Input Data to that Blueprint.

A menu document whose Back action has no key logs a warning when it opens. Keep Confirm and Back out of a document's own mapping context.

The ready-made input assets come with the samples plugin, under /ArcRmlUISamples/Input/ (IA_Sample_Confirm, IA_Sample_Back, IMC_Sample_Common, BP_SampleInputData). A project without its own setup can use them instead of the steps above by adding each block below to the file in its title:

Config/DefaultEngine.ini
[/Script/Engine.Engine]
GameViewportClientClassName=/Script/CommonUI.CommonGameViewportClient
Config/DefaultGame.ini
[/Script/CommonInput.CommonInputSettings]
bEnableEnhancedInputSupport=True
InputData=/ArcRmlUISamples/Input/BP_SampleInputData.BP_SampleInputData_C
Config/DefaultInput.ini
[/Script/Engine.InputSettings]
DefaultPlayerInputClass=/Script/EnhancedInput.EnhancedPlayerInput
DefaultInputComponentClass=/Script/EnhancedInput.EnhancedInputComponent

[/Script/EnhancedInput.EnhancedInputDeveloperSettings]
+DefaultMappingContexts=(InputMappingContext="/ArcRmlUISamples/Input/IMC_Sample_Common.IMC_Sample_Common",Priority=0,bAddImmediately=True,bRegisterWithUserSettings=False)

IMC_Sample_Common maps Enter, Space and gamepad A to IA_Sample_Confirm, Esc and gamepad B to IA_Sample_Back; these lines are the ini form of steps 1, 2, 5, 6 and 8. Restart the editor after changing them. The Input and gamepad page covers navigation, hotkeys and a document's own mapping context.

items.title: Packaging
items.text:
The settings are under Project Settings > Game > ArcRmlUI > Packaging.

  • The folder UI/Rml/Test/ of a content root is never packaged, whatever the settings below say, and the editor does not create a document there.
  • Package Everything on (the default): a packaged build ships every document and style sheet of every content root, compiled.
  • Package Everything off: Paths to Package lists the folders or files to ship (+PathsToPackage=/Game/UI/Rml/Menus in Config/DefaultGame.ini under [/Script/ArcRmlUI.ArcRmlUISettings]). The cook also adds the frames of what it ships (documents that show other documents, see Frames and tabs), the documents that data-action="open:<package path>" names as a literal, and the documents that Blueprints and data assets reference.
  • The font sheets always ship.

items.title: Quick start
items.text: Start here to see a first document open and close with the least setup: the samples plugin and its font sheet. The document is the FirstScreen sample, a title and a line of text with no view model. Install the samples plugin to run it as it is, or copy its files into your own project.

items.title: Before you start
items.text: The ArcRmlUI plugin is enabled in your project (Project setup).

items.title: See plugin content
items.text: The Content Browser shows plugin folders only when its content setting is on. Turn on Plugin Content in the Content Browser's settings menu (the gear button; Settings > Show Plugin Content in the old Content Browser style), then pick the plugin's folder, such as ArcRmlUISamples, under Plugins in the folder tree.

items.title: See it running
items.text:
The samples plugin has C++ code, so the project must be a C++ project.

  1. Copy the ArcRmlUISamples plugin folder into your project's Plugins folder.
  2. In Config/DefaultGame.ini, add the samples' font sheet (the text needs a font, see the warning below): +FontSheets=/ArcRmlUISamples/UI/Rml/Fonts/Fonts.rcss under [/Script/ArcRmlUI.ArcRmlUISettings].
  3. Restart the editor.
  4. Play in the map L_ArcRmlSamples.
  5. Open the console and type:
ArcRmlSamples.Open FirstScreen
  1. You should see a panel at the top left with the title "Hello from ArcRmlUI" and one line of text, as in the picture below. ArcRmlSamples.Close closes it.

Text needs a font

The plugin ships no font. A text element whose font-family names no loaded font draws nothing and logs a warning that starts "No font face defined". Declare a font sheet first (Project setup, Fonts); the samples' sheet is step 2 above.

Without playing, double-click FirstScreen.rml in the Content Browser: the editor preview opens it.

items.title: Open the console
items.text:
The console takes the commands in this guide.

  • In Play In Editor, press the console key (the tilde key by default) and type the command.
  • In the editor, type it in the command box at the bottom of the Output Log window.

ArcRml.Open, ArcRml.Close, ArcRml.Preview, ArcRml.Inspect and the ArcRmlSamples.* commands need Play: without it there is no local player. ArcRml.Validate also runs in the editor's Output Log.

items.title: The document
items.text:
A document is an .rml file with a <head> and a <body>. The <meta> lines in the head say where and how it opens:

  • layer: the layer it opens on, UI.Layer.Game here.
  • input-mode game: the input stays with the game; the document takes no keys or clicks.
FirstScreen.rml
<rml>
<head>
    <title>First screen</title>
    <meta name="layer" content="UI.Layer.Game"/>
    <meta name="input-mode" content="game"/>
    <link type="text/rcss" href="/ArcRmlUISamples/UI/Rml/Shared/Samples.rcss"/>
    <link type="text/rcss" href="FirstScreen.rcss"/>
</head>
<body>
    <div class="fs-panel">
        <h1 class="fs-title">Hello from ArcRmlUI</h1>
        <p>This document has no view model. Game code opens and closes it.</p>
    </div>
</body>
</rml>

A <link> href is a package path or a path relative to the document. The shared sheet sets the text style with the family the samples' font sheet declares:

Shared/Samples.rcss
body, button {
    font-family: 'Arc Samples Sans';
    font-size: 20px;
    color: #e8e8e8;
}
FirstScreen.rcss
.fs-panel {
    position: absolute;
    left: 80px;
    top: 80px;
    padding: 24px 32px;
    background-color: rgba(20, 24, 32, 0.9);
    border-radius: 8px;
}

.fs-title {
    display: block;
    font-size: 36px;
    margin-bottom: 12px;
}

To use the files without the samples plugin, copy them to, for example, Content/UI/Rml/FirstScreen/; the document's path becomes /Game/UI/Rml/FirstScreen/FirstScreen.rml. Then change two things so the text draws:

  • Replace the Samples.rcss link with a style sheet of your own whose font-family names a font declared in your Font Sheets (Project setup, Fonts). The 'Arc Samples Sans' family exists only while the samples' font sheet is listed.
  • Use the new path in the open call of Open and close it instead of /ArcRmlUISamples/UI/Rml/FirstScreen/FirstScreen.rml.

The quickest way to try your own file is the console: ArcRml.Open /Game/UI/Rml/FirstScreen/FirstScreen.rml opens it with no code (Open the console).

items.title: Open and close it
items.text:
Documents open per local player through the UArcRmlViewportSubsystem local player subsystem. OpenDocument takes an FArcRmlDocumentRef, the document's package path, and returns whether it opened; CloseDocument with the same reference closes it.

C++Blueprint FirstScreen/ArcRmlSamplesFirstScreen.cpp
#include "FirstScreen/ArcRmlSamplesFirstScreen.h"

#include "Engine/LocalPlayer.h"
#include "Host/ArcRmlViewportSubsystem.h"

namespace ArcRmlSamplesFirstScreen
{
    FArcRmlDocumentRef Open(ULocalPlayer* LocalPlayer)
    {
        UArcRmlViewportSubsystem* Viewport = LocalPlayer ? LocalPlayer->GetSubsystem<UArcRmlViewportSubsystem>() : nullptr;
        if (!Viewport)
        {
            return FArcRmlDocumentRef();
        }

        const FArcRmlDocumentRef Document{TEXT("/ArcRmlUISamples/UI/Rml/FirstScreen/FirstScreen.rml")};
        return Viewport->OpenDocument(Document) ? Document : FArcRmlDocumentRef();
    }
}

This is an excerpt: it includes the sample's own header, FirstScreen/ArcRmlSamplesFirstScreen.h, which declares Open and includes ArcRmlDocumentRef.h. In your module include ArcRmlDocumentRef.h and declare the function yourself.

To close it, call Viewport->CloseDocument(Document) with the reference Open returned.

Put the function in a module of your project whose Build.cs lists ArcRmlUIData and ArcRmlUI (Project setup), and call it with the local player from your own game code, for example from a PlayerController's BeginPlay with GetLocalPlayer().

Create a Blueprint Function Library asset named BP_FirstScreen_Open with two functions, and call Open with the player controller from the Level Blueprint (Blueprints > Open Level Blueprint in the level editor toolbar), for example from its Event BeginPlay node.

Open (input PlayerController, output Document):

  1. Make Arc Rml Document Ref with Path /ArcRmlUISamples/UI/Rml/FirstScreen/FirstScreen.rml.
  2. Arc Rml Viewport Subsystem (in the palette: Get ArcRmlViewportSubsystem) with the PlayerController input.
  3. Open Document on the subsystem with that Document.
  4. A branch on its return value: when true, the return node outputs the document.

Close (inputs PlayerController, Document):

  1. Arc Rml Viewport Subsystem with the PlayerController input.
  2. Close Document on the subsystem with the Document input.

items.title: Other ways to run it
items.text:
ArcRmlSamples.Open FirstScreen (above) runs the C++ Open. ArcRmlSamples.OpenBP FirstScreen opens it through the Blueprint Open function instead; ArcRmlSamples.Close then calls the Blueprint Close function.

Any document also opens by path from the console: ArcRml.Open /ArcRmlUISamples/UI/Rml/FirstScreen/FirstScreen.rml, and ArcRml.Close with the same path closes it.
